clinicalPearls: An extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of glutamine synthetase
Presents in the neonatal period with severe encephalopathy, hypotonia and intractable seizures
Frequently accompanied by a distinctive necrolytic erythematous skin rash and multi-organ dysfunction
Characteristically shows LOW glutamine in blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, an unusual finding
Moderately raised ammonia may occur despite low glutamine, reflecting impaired ammonia detoxification
The condition is usually fatal in the neonatal period, although rare milder survivors are described
Glutamine is normally the most abundant amino acid, so its deficiency has widespread consequences
reference.pathophysiology: Glutamine synthetase converts glutamate and ammonia into glutamine, a reaction central to nitrogen homeostasis, ammonia detoxification and the supply of glutamine as a nitrogen donor and neurotransmitter precursor. Biallelic loss-of-function GLUL mutations reduce glutamine synthesis, producing systemic and cerebrospinal glutamine deficiency, impaired cerebral ammonia handling and disturbed glutamate-glutamine cycling in the brain. The resulting neuronal dysfunction causes severe neonatal encephalopathy, while deficiency of glutamine as a substrate contributes to the skin and organ involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Maple syrup urine disease and other neonatal metabolic crises
Congenital disorders causing a necrolytic rash
additionalInvestigations: Plasma, urine and cerebrospinal fluid amino acids showing low glutamine
Skin assessment and exclusion of other causes of neonatal rash
redFlags: Severe neonatal encephalopathy with intractable seizures
Necrolytic skin rash in a critically ill neonate
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally very poor, with most affected neonates dying early; a small number of patients with residual enzyme activity have survived with severe neurological impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming amino acid disorders always cause elevated, not reduced, amino acids
Attributing the presentation solely to sepsis
Overlooking glutamine deficiency because routine panels focus on elevations
Missing the diagnostic clue of a necrolytic rash with encephalopathy
references: Textbook of Inborn Metabolic Diseases (standard reference)
management: Provide intensive neonatal supportive care, as there is no established curative therapy for this usually fatal disorder
Trial enteral and parenteral glutamine supplementation to correct the systemic and cerebrospinal glutamine deficiency, as attempted in the rare survivors
Control the intractable neonatal seizures with antiseizure medication and manage the encephalopathy
Reduce ammonia with measures that limit nitrogen load and support detoxification when hyperammonaemia occurs
Give attentive skin care for the necrolytic erythematous rash and manage associated multi-organ dysfunction
Involve the family in early palliative care discussions given the poor prognosis, alongside multidisciplinary metabolic and neonatal input
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, including recurrence risk and prenatal testing
